title: The Mona Lisa Was Missing for Two Years. Did Police Question Picasso?
description:
The common claim is that Picasso was a suspect in the Mona Lisa theft. This episode covers only what the records show. On Monday, August 21, 1911, the Louvre's closing day, the painting was taken in the morning. At 7:30 the next morning a guard saw the empty wall and assumed it had gone to be photographed; the French police's forensic photo shows only four iron hooks left on the wall. On August 29, Paris-Journal printed a thief's confession: he had stolen statues from the Louvre and sold one to "a Parisian painter friend." The poet Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested on September 7. According to Richardson's Picasso biography, at 7 a.m. on September 8 Picasso was taken before an examining magistrate, who asked about the two Iberian stone heads he had bought from Géry Pieret, not about the Mona Lisa; we found no record that he was charged. The painting in fact sat for about two years and three months in the Paris room of a workman, Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught in Florence on December 12, 1913, and the painting was rehung at the Louvre on January 4, 1914. The first court sentenced him to one year and 15 days; at the end of July that year, the appeal cut it to seven months and eight days.

Limits: the story that Picasso told the judge he did not know Apollinaire first appears only in a 1959 newspaper retelling; Apollinaire's 1915 letter says only that the other man "denied knowing" about the affair. None of the 1911 newspapers we searched names Picasso. Why the fingerprints never matched comes from newspapers of the time and later research. Peruggia said he did it for Italy; the appeal court said it was theft all the same. Sources are listed in the references below.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses. Neither the Mona Lisa nor Picasso's works are drawn, nor are modern researchers.

Information as of 2026-10-20

ml101.text: Tuesday, August 22, 1911: the Salon Carré at the Louvre in Paris.

ml102.text: Béroud, a regular copyist, reportedly set up his easel;

ml103.text: but on the wall before him, only four iron hooks remained.

ml104.text: What used to hang there was the Mona Lisa.

ml106.text: at 2 p.m., police at the door gave passersby a reason for closing;

ml107.text: a self-styled thief delivered a Louvre statue to a newspaper;

ml108.text: later, the police came for the painter Picasso;

ml109.text: and on the glass over the painting was one fingerprint.

ml110.text: In the Mona Lisa’s two missing years, did police question Picasso?

ml201.text: In fact, a guard saw the bare wall at 7:30 a.m.;

ml202.text: he thought it was out for a photo.

ml203.text: Only when the photographer came and didn’t have it did panic set in.

ml204.text: At 12:30, Prefect of Police Lépine arrived and sealed off the whole museum.

ml205.text: The empty frame turned up on a service staircase, without a scratch.

ml206.text: At 2 p.m., visitors were politely shown out;

ml207.text: police at the door said a pipe had burst.

ml208.text: But when exactly had the painting vanished?

ml210.text: the Louvre’s one closed day a week. No visitors, only cleaners and workmen.

ml211.text: Per examining magistrate Drioux’s later inquiry, at 7:15 that morning,

ml212.text: a house painter pointed to a big canvas nearby:

ml213.text: “And the little one’s worth more! They say it’s the dearest in the museum.”

ml214.text: Around 7:20, a plumber found a door to the courtyard standing open,

ml215.text: its lock tampered with, one knob missing.

ml216.text: Then at 8:15, when two of the foreman’s men passed again, the wall was bare.

ml217.text: One said, “They’ve taken it already.” The other: “Must be the works.”

ml218.text: What did Parisians say first at the news?

ml301.text: Many asked if the thief had taken Notre-Dame’s towers too.

ml302.text: A Paris-Journal headline asked: is Arsène Lupin alive?

ml303.text: The paper also offered a 50,000-franc reward, no names asked.

ml304.text: On August 29, the Louvre reopened. Everyone went first to the Salon Carré

ml305.text: to stare at the gap and discuss the theft;

ml306.text: a later book says more people than usual came to gape at those four hooks.

ml307.text: Remember the thief who brought a statue to the paper?

ml308.text: On reopening day, Paris-Journal ran his confession:

ml309.text: he said another one he stole years ago went to a painter friend in Paris,

ml310.text: who paid him a little, about 50 francs, which he lost that night at billiards.

ml311.text: Who was this painter friend in Paris?

ml401.text: Picasso. But that name was added later by biographers;

ml402.text: the papers of the day that we found never name him.

ml405.text: Picasso had bought from him two Iberian stone heads stolen from the Louvre.

ml406.text: His girlfriend recalled him and Apollinaire taking a suitcase at night

ml407.text: to dump the statues in the Seine; at 2 a.m. they were back, suitcase and all.

ml408.text: On September 5, Apollinaire handed the statues to Paris-Journal.

ml409.text: On the night of September 7, 1911, he was arrested for “harboring a criminal.”

ml410.text: Yet the papers said he was held on suspicion over the Mona Lisa’s disappearance;

ml411.text: he later wrote: police took him thinking he knew where the Mona Lisa was.

ml412.text: Jailed in La Santé, he wrote: I am No. 15 of the 11th block.

ml413.text: Remember the police coming for Picasso?

ml414.text: Next day: per his biography, at 7 a.m. on September 8, he was taken to a magistrate.

ml415.text: His girlfriend said he shook so badly she had to help him dress.

ml416.text: Before the judge, he faced Apollinaire, who was in handcuffs.

ml417.text: Did the judge ask about the Mona Lisa?

ml418.text: No. He asked about the two stone heads Picasso bought; the possible charge: receiving stolen goods.

ml419.text: Afterward he went home, told only not to leave Paris for now.

ml420.text: Legend has Picasso telling the judge: “I’ve never seen this man.”

ml421.text: That line traces back no further than a 1959 newspaper retelling.

ml422.text: What did Apollinaire, who was there, write?

ml423.text: His 1915 letter says only: the other man denied knowing about it.

ml424.text: On September 12 he was freed for now; leading French writers had petitioned for him.

ml425.text: The poet and the painter had both been questioned. So where was the Mona Lisa?

ml501.text: Right in Paris, in a workman’s room, where it stayed for about two years and three months.

ml502.text: He was Peruggia, an Italian once hired by the Louvre to put protective glass on paintings.

ml503.text: The magistrate had in fact questioned him that year;

ml504.text: he admitted coming in two hours late that morning;

ml505.text: police wrote asking for his fingerprints; he never replied.

ml506.text: Remember the fingerprint on the glass?

ml507.text: Peruggia’s prints were already on file: he’d been arrested before and printed twice.

ml508.text: So why was there never a match?

ml509.text: Later research says the cards were filed by body measurements, not fingerprints;

ml510.text: Bertillon himself said his staff was too small to search.

ml511.text: He also made a white wooden box with a false bottom to keep it in.

ml512.text: In July 1913, he went to a London dealer to sell it;

ml513.text: but the dealer just told him: give it back to the Louvre.

ml514.text: That November, he saw an ad placed by Florence antiques dealer Geri

ml515.text: and wrote to him as “Leonard V.”;

ml516.text: he offered him first pick, at 25 percent off.

ml517.text: Would he really walk into that shop with the painting?

ml518.text: He did. On December 10 he reached Florence, checked into a hotel and went to Geri’s shop that day;

ml519.text: back the next afternoon, he found Uffizi director Poggi already there.

ml520.text: It came out of the hotel trunk; blaming poor light, the director took it to the Uffizi.

ml521.text: Then on the afternoon of December 12, still waiting for Geri’s answer, he was arrested.

ml522.text: He confessed at once: he’d acted alone,

ml523.text: and it was revenge for what was looted under Napoleon.

ml524.text: So how did he get it out?

ml525.text: He said he came in by the workers’ entrance just after 7 and took the painting off the wall,

ml526.text: unframed it in the stairwell and wrapped it in his work smock.

ml527.text: The door missing a knob fits too: he had taken the knob off, and an unwitting worker even opened the door for him.

ml528.text: He admitted he’d looked around the Salon Carré that morning and chose it just for its size.

ml529.text: Prints from his old case matched those on the frame and glass exactly.

ml530.text: It was shown at the Uffizi for five days; 30,000 people crowded in on day one.

ml532.text: On January 4, 1914, the painting was hung back in place;

ml533.text: that morning, fewer than 60 people were there to greet it.

ml534.text: That June, a court in Florence gave Peruggia one year and 15 days.

ml536.text: but the court produced his letter to his father: a fortune, it said, was on its way.

ml538.text: In late July the appeal said: even to hang it in Italy, it was theft;

ml539.text: the sentence was cut to seven months and eight days, already served in custody.

ml540.text: Remember Picasso at 7 that morning? We found no record of him being charged. This file is closed.
